item.title: The Face That Tricks Every Pet Parent
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The classic "guilty look" you see in dogs is almost certainly not actual guilt, according to the best current research; it is a set of appeasement behaviors that they use to de-escalate perceived conflict with their humans
  • A landmark 2009 study found that dogs display "guilty" body language based on how their owners behave, not on whether the dog has actually done anything wrong
  • Guilt is a self-conscious emotion requiring the ability to reflect on past actions and feel remorse, and it is a cognitively complex process not well-supported by current evidence in dogs
  • After-the-fact punishment does not teach dogs anything about their earlier behavior — it just teaches them that owners can be unpredictably scary, sometimes leading to hidden accidents or increased anxiety
  • The effective approach is management, catching them in the act with calm redirection, positive reinforcement, and staying neutral when discovering a mess

You come home, and something is off. Maybe it is the shreds of couch cushion on the floor, or the puddle by the back door, or the pillow that used to have stuffing in it.

Then you see them. Your dog, slinking toward you with head lowered, ears flattened, eyes averted, and a full-body posture that screams: I know I did something bad.

It is one of the most universally recognized expressions in the dog world. And it is also, according to the best current research, almost certainly not what you think it is.

Do Dogs Actually Feel Guilt?

First, let us give dogs the emotional credit they deserve. Research confirms that dogs feel a range of real emotions including joy, fear, love, and anger. Anyone who has lived with one knows this in their bones.

But guilt is a specific and more complex emotion than any of those. In humans, guilt is what psychologists call a self-conscious emotion. It requires the ability to reflect on your own actions, recognize you have broken a rule, and feel remorse about it. That involves a kind of moral self-awareness tied to higher-order thinking.

Shame is a close cousin. In humans, shame is about the self (“I am bad”), while guilt is about the act (“I did something bad”). Neither is well-supported by current evidence as a conscious experience dogs actually have.

What dogs do experience, researchers suggest, is something more immediate and social: a response to cues in their environment, especially the emotional cues coming from their human. That is a quite different mechanism from remorse.1

Some veterinary experts frame this as a classic case of anthropomorphism — the very human tendency to attribute our own characteristics and emotions to animals. It comes from a place of love, but it can also lead us to misread what our dogs are actually telling us.2

The Famous Guilty-Look Study

The most-cited study on this question comes from cognitive scientist Dr. Alexandra Horowitz at Barnard College, published in 2009 in Behavioral Processes.3 Horowitz set up trials in which dog owners either correctly or incorrectly believed their dog had eaten a forbidden treat. She then observed how the dogs behaved when their owners returned. The results were striking.4

Dogs displayed “guilty” behaviors — lowered heads, flattened ears, averted eyes — based on how the owners behaved, not on whether the dog had actually done anything wrong. Innocent dogs who were scolded showed just as much guilty-looking body language as dogs who had truly eaten the treat.5

Horowitz’s conclusion was careful and worth quoting: “A better description of the so-called guilty look is that it is a response to owner cues, rather than that it shows an appreciation of a misdeed.”

Notably, Horowitz herself has said her study was not designed to definitively prove that dogs do not feel guilt. “I would feel dreadful if people then thought the case was closed on dogs (not) feeling guilt, which is definitely not the case,” she said.6

The honest answer, based on the current science, is that the classic guilty look certainly is not guilt — but we cannot say for sure what dogs are subjectively feeling. What we can say is that the face they make when caught has a much simpler explanation.

What the Guilty Look Really Is

What we read as guilt is actually a well-documented set of appeasement behaviors. These are social signals that say, in canine language, “I mean no harm, please don't be angry with me.” The classic guilty look includes some combination of:7,8,9

  • A lowered head
  • Flattened or pinned-back ears
  • Averted eyes or refusal to make eye contact
  • A tucked tail (or a tail thumping the floor from a lowered posture)
  • Lip licking
  • Yawning
  • Whale eye (the whites of the eyes visible)
  • Hunched or lowered body posture
  • Cowering or retreating

These are all appeasement and stress signals. They are deeply ingrained social behaviors inherited from wolves, used to manage relationships and reduce social tension. When your dog senses that you are upset, tense, or angry, they use these signals in an attempt to calm the situation.

Dogs Are Reading You, Not Themselves

Here is what makes this so persuasive. Dogs are extraordinarily skilled at reading human body language, facial expressions, and tone of voice. Research has found they are actually better at reading us than our closest primate relatives are.10

When you walk into a room and your shoulders tense, your brow furrows, and your voice deepens, your dog notices it immediately. They notice the shift long before you have finished processing it consciously. The guilty look is their response to you — not to what they did an hour ago. It is a communication move, not a confession.

Every household has its own set of unwritten rules — what counts as “good” or “bad” behavior varies from home to home. Dogs come into these arrangements with no innate knowledge of your rules. They learn what you prefer through consistent training and consistent consequences, not through some inner moral compass. That is why the same dog can look “guilty” for something that would be perfectly acceptable in another home.11

Why the Look Develops

If the guilty look is not actual guilt, why does it come out so reliably in certain situations? The answer is classical and operant conditioning — the same learning mechanisms that shape most dog behavior.

Dogs are pattern-recognition experts. Over time, they learn to associate specific situations with specific outcomes. A dog who has been scolded for coming home to find a chewed-up cushion starts to associate coming home + chewed-up cushion + owner arriving with a negative reaction.

Crucially, the dog is not connecting their earlier chewing with the punishment. They are connecting the current environmental context (owner arriving, mess on floor) with what usually happens next (unpleasant interaction).

Over time, with repetition, that anticipation becomes a reliable, conditioned response. The guilty look then shows up preemptively any time those conditions are present — regardless of whether the dog has actually done anything wrong.

This helps explain some real-life head-scratchers. In multi-dog households, sometimes the guilty-looking dog is the innocent one — the peacemaker of the pair, who reads the tension and tries to de-escalate.12,13

Dogs Live in the Present

item.title: Watch Out for This Synthetic Vitamin — It's a Liver Toxin
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Menadione and menadione sodium bisulfite complex (MSBC), synthetic forms of vitamin K, are widely used in pet food though they are only approved for use in poultry feeds
  • Menadione and MSBC can be found in all types of pet food, including a few commercial raw diets, so regardless of the type of pet food you buy, it’s important to check labels carefully for the presence of this synthetic nutrient
  • Pet food producers use menadione because it’s an inexpensive and stable ingredient, however, it lacks many of the important properties of natural vitamin K derived from whole foods
  • Menadione has been identified as a liver toxin; even in very small amounts, ingestion of this synthetic vitamin on a daily basis over a dog’s or cat’s lifetime is cause for concern
  • Synthetic nutrients like menadione often have a different molecular structure than their natural counterparts, making them less efficiently used by the body and creating additional waste for the body to process

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published June 30, 2020.

Menadione, a synthetic form of vitamin K, is a widely used ingredient in pet food. According to PetfoodIndustry.com, from a strictly regulatory standpoint, there’s been no issue for decades with this additive. Both menadione and menadione sodium bisulfite complex (MSBC) are allowed in pet foods as “vitamin K active substances,” even though the FDA has sanctioned their use in poultry feeds only.1

Unsurprisingly, even though these faux versions of vitamin K are allowed only in poultry feed, the FDA notes on its website that they’re widely used in feeds for other species, including pet foods. As board-certified veterinary nutritionist Dr. David Dzanis explains in an article:

“… despite lacking formal approval, this reference to their use for feeds other than for poultry without explicit objection has allowed regulators to exercise enforcement discretion and tolerate the unfettered use of MSBC in pet foods.”2

Menadione and MSBC are two more unapproved additives with toxicity concerns that are found in pet food in flagrant violation of regulations prohibiting their use. According to Dzanis, "at least one state feed control official has taken action against any pet product containing MSBC."

Apparently, the state for which this feed control official works uses a more literal interpretation of “unapproved for use” than is the norm. Said another way, as the state sees it, “no means no” with regard to the use of menadione/MSBC in pet food.

This presents quite a snafu for pet food manufacturers who sell products containing MSBC in that particular state:

“Urging of the state to exercise enforcement discretion in this instance, or other quick regulatory fixes, such as amendment to the AAFCO listing, appear to be at a stalemate,” Dzanis writes.

Types of Pet Foods Containing Menadione

Veterinarian Dr. Tom Cameron, interviewed on this topic in 2015, has found synthetic vitamin K in every type of pet food, including raw, but its use is especially prevalent in dry and canned foods. Even proponents of raw diets may be surprised to discover menadione is used in some commercial raw pet foods.

Most people who advocate raw diets understand that consuming food in its natural form and freshly prepared is optimally healthy. Finding menadione in raw diets indicates that some companies aren’t investigating the ingredients they use. They’re placing their trust in their formulators without actually evaluating each individual ingredient in their food, which is concerning.

So, for all of you out there who haven’t read the fine print on your pet food label — even if you’re buying an excellent quality raw diet — be sure to examine the list of vitamins and minerals closely. If you see menadione or vitamin K3 on the list, you know the food contains a possibly toxic ingredient. For more information on menadione, read this excellent Dog Food Advisor article.

Why Pet Food Producers Use Menadione

The primary reason ultraprocessed pet food producers use menadione is that it’s an inexpensive and stable ingredient. It’s much cheaper to make synthetic vitamin K3 in a laboratory than to use natural food-based forms of vitamin K, and cost is a primary driver in pet food manufacturing.

In addition, menadione is a very stable ingredient. Unlike natural vitamins, it isn’t affected by heat, sunlight, storage, dehydration or other factors. Using whole food ingredients in pet food in a way that keeps them stable is a more involved process. Plus, whole food ingredients are more expensive.

Some pet food manufacturers claim they’re using menadione at very low levels, but as Dr. Cameron explains, the difference is that most dogs and cats eat processed pet food their entire lives — sometimes 13, 14, 15 years or longer.

Even a small amount of a toxic substance given for a decade or two is cause for concern. In veterinary practice, many different conditions related to the organs of detoxification are observed. Given the barrage of environmental chemicals pets are exposed to, feeding small amounts of known toxins over a long period of time may be adding to the problem and contributing to the dozens of degenerative diseases seen today.

Menadione May Be Toxic to the Liver and Other Organs

Menadione is a synthetic analog, which means it’s man-made. Natural vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin that is absorbed through fat metabolism. Menadione is a water-soluble form of vitamin K that works very differently. It is presumably absorbed by bacteria in the gut and converted to forms of vitamin K the body can use.

There are very significant limitations to menadione vs. natural vitamin K. For example, it doesn’t support blood clotting. There are important properties of natural vitamin K that synthetic vitamin K lacks.

Another significant and growing concern about menadione is that it may cause liver toxicity. According to Dr. Cameron, there are many references that classify menadione as a toxin. There are studies from other countries that show that menadione causes toxicity to liver cells and red blood cells.

There are also material safety data sheets (MSDS) that list menadione as a substance that is toxic to the liver, kidneys, lungs, mucous membranes, and other tissues.3 Obviously, it’s a concern when a toxin is being added to foods that pets are fed every day.

What Are the Long-Term Health Effects of Synthetic Nutrients?

Our pets’ bodies (and ours) have evolved over millions of years eating whole foods and efficiently processing nutrients from those foods. There are very specific receptors in the body that are designed to make perfect use of the nutrients contained in real food.

When whole foods are broken apart to reproduce their nutrients in the laboratory, significant limitations arise. When a synthetic nutrient is created in a lab, the finished product has a different structure from the natural form of the nutrient. Generally speaking, a man-made nutrient doesn’t fit well into the receptor in the body that was designed for that nutrient in its natural state.

The result is that not all components of the synthetic nutrient can be used by the body. It is therefore less efficient, it doesn’t have the same metabolic effect as the real thing, and the body has to process the unusable portion as a xenobiotic (waste) product. It takes energy to get rid of the waste, which is a drain on the body’s resources.

Some nutrients such as zinc are hard to come by in whole food sources. In these cases, many human grade pet food companies resort to using human quality supplements to supply the handful of mineral deficits commonly found in fresh commercial pet diets. The quality of lab-made nutrients ranges from contaminated to highly purified, unabsorbable to highly absorbable.

Thankfully, amino acid chelates and proteinates provide better absorption and assimilation than many of the cheaper “feed grade” minerals, including the oxides and sulfates found on ingredient panels that pet owners would be best to avoid. In the case of vitamin K, there are safer and healthier choices when it comes to supplementation, but feed grade pet food companies don’t want to spend the money on the more expensive options.

Menadione is a vitamin K analog — a synthetic version of vitamin K. Many people know that vitamin K comes from certain foods, for example, green leafy vegetables and liver. Vitamin K is an important factor in blood clotting. It also drives minerals to certain organs of the body like the teeth and bones, to help them heal and to support connective tissue.

Menadione is called vitamin K3 and as discussed above, it’s widely used in pet foods to replace naturally occurring vitamin K in order to meet AAFCO nutrient profile standards. For several years now, there’s been a good deal of controversy and concern around the use of this substance in pet food.

According to Dr. Cameron, there are human studies that show long-term use of synthetic vitamins does not have the expected health benefits. When a nutrient is fractioned and separated from all the other ingredients that create synergy and work together with it, the therapeutic activity of the nutrient is lost.

As with many questionable ingredients in the food supply — another is sodium selenite (synthetic selenium) — there’s an ongoing debate about whether or not they are safe. No long-term safety studies have been done with pets. The healthier and safer approach is to get the bulk of nutrients, especially vitamins and minerals, from food rather than supplements — in particular poor quality, “feed grade” synthetic supplements.

Sources and References

  • 1,2 PetfoodIndustry.com, April 1, 2020
  • 3 MSDS Vitamin K3

Menadione is a synthetic analog, which means it’s man-made. Natural vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin that is absorbed through fat metabolism. Menadione is a water-soluble form of vitamin K that works very differently. It is presumably absorbed by bacteria in the gut and converted to forms of vitamin K the body can use.

What Are the Long-Term Health Effects of Synthetic Nutrients?

Our pets’ bodies (and ours) have evolved over millions of years eating whole foods and efficiently processing nutrients from those foods. There are very specific receptors in the body that are designed to make perfect use of the nutrients contained in real food.

When whole foods are broken apart to reproduce their nutrients in the laboratory, significant limitations arise. When a synthetic nutrient is created in a lab, the finished product has a different structure from the natural form of the nutrient. Generally speaking, a man-made nutrient doesn’t fit well into the receptor in the body that was designed for that nutrient in its natural state.

The result is that not all components of the synthetic nutrient can be used by the body. It is therefore less efficient, it doesn’t have the same metabolic effect as the real thing, and the body has to process the unusable portion as a xenobiotic (waste) product. It takes energy to get rid of the waste, which is a drain on the body’s resources.

Some nutrients such as zinc are hard to come by in whole food sources. In these cases, many human grade pet food companies resort to using human quality supplements to supply the handful of mineral deficits commonly found in fresh commercial pet diets. The quality of lab-made nutrients ranges from contaminated to highly purified, unabsorbable to highly absorbable.

Thankfully, amino acid chelates and proteinates provide better absorption and assimilation than many of the cheaper “feed grade” minerals, including the oxides and sulfates found on ingredient panels that pet owners would be best to avoid. In the case of vitamin K, there are safer and healthier choices when it comes to supplementation, but feed grade pet food companies don’t want to spend the money on the more expensive options.

Menadione is a vitamin K analog — a synthetic version of vitamin K. Many people know that vitamin K comes from certain foods, for example, green leafy vegetables and liver. Vitamin K is an important factor in blood clotting. It also drives minerals to certain organs of the body like the teeth and bones, to help them heal and to support connective tissue.

Menadione is called vitamin K3 and as discussed above, it’s widely used in pet foods to replace naturally occurring vitamin K in order to meet AAFCO nutrient profile standards. For several years now, there’s been a good deal of controversy and concern around the use of this substance in pet food.

According to Dr. Cameron, there are human studies that show long-term use of synthetic vitamins does not have the expected health benefits. When a nutrient is fractioned and separated from all the other ingredients that create synergy and work together with it, the therapeutic activity of the nutrient is lost.

As with many questionable ingredients in the food supply — another is sodium selenite (synthetic selenium) — there’s an ongoing debate about whether or not they are safe. No long-term safety studies have been done with pets. The healthier and safer approach is to get the bulk of nutrients, especially vitamins and minerals, from food rather than supplements — in particular poor quality, “feed grade” synthetic supplements.

item.title: The Aquarium Crew That Doesn't Include a Single Fish
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • People watching an aquarium had reductions in heart rate, increases in mood, and other signs of improved well-being
  • Popular non-fish aquarium pets include various types of turtles, salamanders, toads, crabs, snails, and even shrimp
  • Aquarium pets do require regular attention, upkeep, and stimulation to be healthy and happy
  • Some species have remarkable traits — axolotls, for example, can regenerate limbs and even parts of their brain 
  • Aquarium pet needs vary widely by species, from brackish water for red-clawed crabs to a half land, half water setup for fire-bellied toads, making species-specific research essential before bringing one home 

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published August 29, 2015.

If you'd like to add a pet to your home but perhaps don't want quite the commitment of adding a cat, dog, or bird, an aquarium pet may be for you. Be aware, aquarium pets do require regular attention, upkeep, and stimulation to be healthy and happy, however they can be good options for people who are away from home during the day.

Aquarium pets can also be quite good for your health. For instance, people viewing a large aquarium exhibit had reductions in heart rate, increases in mood, and other signs of improved well-being.1

It's well known that exposure to natural environments has calming and stress-reducing effects in humans, and viewing an aquarium may be an extension of this. Some people are also simply drawn to the types of pets that aquariums house — amphibians are a particularly popular choice — and it's far more than just fish.

9 Non-Fish Aquarium Pets

Thinking of adding an aquarium to your home but looking for a pet other than fish? Check out these unique pet options compiled by Mom.me:2

  1. Axolotl — Axolotls are fascinating salamanders native to Mexico. They have the astounding ability to regenerate parts of their bodies, including limbs and even their brain. Axolotls require ample space to move around in, so yours will need at least a 20-gallon tank. And they're messy — so plan on cleaning the tank frequently and performing regular maintenance.


  2. Fire-bellied newt — Fire-bellied newts have striking orange bellies that secrete a skin-irritating toxin (this is why you should always wear gloves when handling one). The aquarium needs to be carefully divided to provide about 70% water and the rest sloping land area, or alternatively full water with floating cork bark for your newt to rest on.

    Newts need ample stimulation and attention to habitat, such as the addition of aquatic plants, stones, and logs for climbing and hiding.
  3. Ghost shrimp — These freshwater shrimp are often purchased as food for fish and other aquarium pets, but they make great pets in their own right. Their bodies are nearly transparent, making them interesting to look at, and they're easy to care for.

    Populating your aquarium with appropriate plants will keep your ghost shrimp happy (and the family is likely to grow, as ghost shrimp easily spawn in aquariums).
  4. Sea monkey — Sea monkeys were heavily marketed to kids over the years, but these brine shrimp actually do make great pets (albeit they don't look much like the "sea monkey" advertisements suggest). Brine shrimp eggs can be dried and remain viable for years, hatching only after you add water. The baby brine shrimps then grow to maturity in just one week.
  5. Freshwater snail — Snails can co-exist with other aquarium pets or be your featured inhabitant. Popular options include apple snails, mystery snails, inca snails, nerite snails, and rabbit snails. Every two to four weeks, you'll need to replace 10% to 25% of your snail's water, and be sure you have a tight-fitting lid, since snails can easily scale walls and escape.
  6. Red-clawed crab — These bold crabs are beautiful to look at but will pinch aggressively when handled. Their strong personalities only add to their charm, though, and they're relatively easy to care for. Red-clawed crabs need semi-salty (brackish) water in the aquarium, along with a few perches above the water line to rest. A tight lid is essential to prevent escape.
  7. Fire-bellied toad — Like the fire-bellied newt, the fire-bellied toad boasts a striking orange-red belly that also secretes toxins into the water. The water needs to be changed frequently to prevent build-up from harming the toad. Fire-bellied toads need a mix of land and water in the tank (about half and half) to explore.


  8. Freshwater crayfish — Crayfish do well living with their own kind, but with more than 100 species to choose from, you'll need to do your research to find out which habitat is best. Most can live in a 5- to 10-gallon tank, although a larger tank is necessary for multiple crayfish. While crayfish make interesting pets, they are messy eaters and tend to hide food, so plan on frequent water changes.
  9. Red-eared slider turtle — The red-eared slider is the most popular aquatic/semi-aquatic pet turtle. Most of the aquarium should contain fresh, frequently changed water, although this turtle also needs a basking area to warm itself (under a heat lamp).

Sources and References

  • 1 Environment & Behavior July 28, 2015
  • 2 Mom.me February 26, 2015

item.title: Crocodiles' Eyes Are Uniquely Suited for Ambush Hunting
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Crocodile eyes have a horizontal streak of tightly packed receptors called fovea
  • The fovea are typically located in a circular area, but in crocodiles the horizontal streak gives them the advantage of being able to scan the shoreline for prey without moving their head
  • Crocodile eyes also correspond with their habitat’s lighting conditions; freshwater crocs were more sensitive to redder wavelengths of light found in freshwater habitats
  • Crocodile vision is up to seven times less precise than human vision overall, but the foveal streak gives them a strong advantage in spotting prey along the horizon
  • Crocodiles and alligators are among a very small group of species — along with primates, dolphins and killer whales — observed using coordination and collaboration to hunt prey

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published November 15, 2016.

Crocodiles are one of the world's greatest ambush predators. They lack the endurance for long chases on land or in the water, so instead they depend on launching surprise attacks on their prey.

Crocodiles lie in wait, camouflaged in the water, until an opportunity presents itself. These indiscriminate eaters will attack virtually anything for a meal — zebras, hippos, birds, porcupines, fish, crabs, small mammals and even people are all fair game for a crocodile.

At the first glimpse of a meal, the crocodile explodes into action, lunging for and typically catching its prey in one swift movement, often before the prey has a chance to react.

Crocodiles are believed to be largely unchanged from their prehistoric ancestors (dinosaurs), but they do have some unique features that make them remarkably adept at their sneak attacks. Research shows even their eyes are fine-tuned for lurking.

Crocodile Eyes Are Uniquely Suited for Lurking

Crocodiles lie in the water seemingly motionless, which is a key part of their hunting strategy. They stay so still that they blend in easily with their environment and unsuspecting prey may swim right by. Their eyes are uniquely suited for this long-term lurking.

Research published in the Journal of Experimental Biology found crocodile eyes have a horizontal streak of tightly packed receptors called fovea.

The fovea are typically located in a circular area, but in crocodiles the horizontal streak gives them the advantage of being able to scan the shoreline for prey without moving their head.

Fovea are used for high-resolution viewing. In humans, for instance, the fovea is used to read, but because the fovea only exist in a small area, the eyes need to move to see larger areas. Nicolas Nagloo, study author and Ph.D. student at the University of Western Australia, told BBC News:1

"Typically, the fovea is circular and located in the center of the retina. It provides animals with an area of very high visual clarity, in a small area of their visual environment …
In the case of crocodiles ... it's spread across the middle of the retina, and it gives them maximum clarity all along the visual horizon."

Overall, it's believed that crocodile vision is up to seven times less precise than human vision, but the high-clarity "foveal streak" gives them a strong advantage in finding prey.

Crocodile Eyes Are Adapted for Different Water Conditions

Other unique features were also noted in crocodile eyes, specifically in relation to their salt and freshwater habitats. Saltwater tends to have more blue light while freshwater has more red light.

The study found that crocodile eyes corresponded with their habitat's lighting conditions; freshwater crocs were more sensitive to redder wavelengths of light than saltwater crocs.

The finding is especially intriguing because crocodiles have blurry vision underwater, and it wasn't thought vision was an important sense for them while swimming. Nagloo told BBC News that this assumption may need to be investigated:2

"It's surprising because these guys can't actually focus underwater. [But] light sensitivity seems to be important to them … That tells us there's potentially some aspect of their behavior underwater that we're not aware of yet."

Do Crocodiles Hunt in Groups?

Only a select group of species is known to engage in coordinated hunting efforts. This includes certain primates, bottlenose dolphins, killer whales and two species of fish.

Whether or not other species engage in this seemingly rare behavior is unknown, in large part because it's difficult to observe animals hunting in their natural environment.

This is especially true of crocodilians (crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials), as they typically hunt at night in murky waters in remote swamps and rivers. Further, they eat infrequently, which makes witnessing hunting efforts even more challenging.

Dr. Vladimir Dinets of the University of Tennessee in Knoxville used a combination of eyewitness accounts from amateurs and researchers, 3,000 hours of observations and diary accounts dating back to the 19th century to learn more about crocodilian hunting behaviors.3

What he uncovered is that most of the observations had a common thread — crocodiles (and alligators) use coordination and collaboration when hunting their prey.

Crocodiles have been observed swimming in circles around fish in order to force them into a tight "bait ball" and then taking turns swimming through the bait ball for a snack.

In another instance, a crocodile on land scared a pig into a lagoon where two other crocodiles were waiting in ambush. Crocodiles have also been known to chase fish toward shore where smaller crocodiles were waiting. Dinets told Science News:4

"All these observations indicate that crocodilians might belong to a very select club of hunters — just twenty or so species of animals, including humans — capable of coordinating their actions in sophisticated ways and assuming different roles according to each individual's abilities. … In fact, they might be second only to humans in their hunting prowess."

Do Crocodiles Live in the US?

American crocodiles are considered an endangered species. The only remaining American crocodiles in the U.S. live in southern Florida, while most others are found in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America.5

Habitat loss, illegal hunting and roadkill present serious threats to American crocodiles. The Nile crocodile, found in Africa, is also facing population declines due to pollution, hunting and habitat loss.6 In case you were wondering, you can distinguish a crocodile from an alligator by the fourth tooth on the bottom of the jaw; it's visible on crocodiles when their mouths are closed.7

Sources and References

  • The Journal of Experimental Biology May 1, 2016
  • 1,2 BBC News May 4, 2016
  • 3 Ethology Ecology & Evolution 2015 Vol. 27, No. 2, 244-250
  • 4 Science News October 14, 2014
  • 5,7 Defenders of Wildlife, Crocodile
  • 6 National Geographic, Nile Crocodile

item.title: Could Your Pet's Clean-Up Crew Use a Hand?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The lymphatic system is your dog's internal drainage and immune network that carries lymph fluid, clears cellular waste, transports fats and immune cells, and helps launch immune responses when threats appear
  • Unlike blood circulation, the lymphatic system has no pump; it relies entirely on muscle contraction, movement, breathing, and hydration to keep lymph flowing
  • Signs of a sluggish lymphatic system can be subtle and easy to miss: chronic skin issues, recurring infections, slow wound healing, low energy, puffy lymph nodes, and persistent yeast or bacterial problems are all worth paying attention to
  • The highest-impact supports are the simplest ones: daily movement (walks, gentle play, swimming), consistent hydration, moisture-rich whole foods, and reducing the toxic load coming in from processed food, tap water, and unnecessary household chemicals
  • Complementary strategies can add real value, like gentle skin brushing and lymphatic massage toward the heart, lymph-supportive herbs (under veterinary guidance), acupuncture, and adequate rest

If your dog seems a little sluggish lately, keeps getting the same skin issues, or takes longer to bounce back from a minor injury, there's a system inside them doing a lot of quiet work that rarely gets mentioned. It has no dedicated pump, no glamorous imagery, and no household name.

It's the lymphatic system. And while most pet parents can name the heart or the liver in a heartbeat, this one usually gets skipped. That's a shame, because supporting a dog's lymphatic system is one of the most underappreciated things you can do for their long-term health.

What the Lymphatic System Actually Does

Think of the lymphatic system as your dog’s internal drainage and immune network. It’s a web of vessels, nodes, and organs that moves a clear-to-milky fluid called lymph through the body. Lymph carries white blood cells, proteins, fats, and cellular waste. Key parts of the system include:1,2,3

  • Lymph vessels that carry lymph fluid throughout the body
  • Lymph nodes, which cluster under the jaw, in the armpits, groin, and other spots, act as checkpoints that filter and screen for threats
  • The spleen, which filters blood and lymph
  • The thymus, which trains immune cells (especially in young animals)
  • Tonsils and adenoids, which protect entry points like the mouth and nose

The system's job list is impressive. It clears out waste, transports fats from the digestive tract, produces antibodies, delivers nutrients to muscles and tissues, and helps launch immune responses when pathogens show up. Some call it the body's garbage truck, but that undersells it; it's more like the sanitation crew, quality-control team, and rapid-response unit rolled into one.

Why It Needs Your Help

Here’s the catch: Unlike the circulatory system, which has the heart to push blood around, the lymphatic system has no central pump. It relies entirely on muscle contraction, movement, breathing, and hydration to keep lymph flowing.4,5

That means dogs who are sedentary, dehydrated, recovering from illness, or under chronic stress are more likely to have sluggish lymph flow. And when lymph gets stagnant, the whole cleanup process slows down. Waste builds up, inflammation rises, and immunity dips.

This isn’t a fringe idea. Movement, hydration, and reducing toxic load are the pillars of a well-functioning lymphatic system. The good news is that all three are within your reach.

Signs Your Dog’s Lymphatic System May Be Sluggish

A quietly under-functioning lymphatic system can produce a scattered set of symptoms that are easy to attribute to something else. Some of the more common signs include:6,7,8

  • Chronic skin issues, hotspots, or itchiness
  • Recurring infections
  • Slow wound healing
  • Swollen or puffy lymph nodes, especially under the jaw or in the groin
  • Swelling in the limbs or face
  • Lethargy or low energy
  • Persistent yeast or bacterial issues
  • Frequent eye drainage or crusty skin
  • Joint stiffness or discomfort

Dogs with allergies, autoimmune conditions, or chronic inflammation are particularly prone to lymphatic congestion.

  • Daily walks, even short ones
  • Gentle play sessions like fetch or tug
  • Stretching and bowing are natural lymph-friendly motions dogs do on their own
  • Swimming or hydrotherapy, especially for senior dogs or those with joint issues
  • Sniffing walks that combine mental and physical engagement

  • Provide clean, filtered water throughout the day.
  • Add moisture to meals with bone broth, gently cooked food, or fresh options.
  • Watch for signs of dehydration — dry gums, thick saliva, and less-elastic skin.
  • Consider a water source you’d be willing to drink yourself, since heavy metals, chlorine, and other contaminants add to the body’s toxin load.

Diet and the Toxic Load

What goes into the body affects how hard the lymphatic system has to work to clean up. Diets heavy in ultraprocessed ingredients, artificial additives, and low-quality fillers give the body more junk to process.

A cleaner, whole-food-oriented diet — real proteins, fresh vegetables, and some moisture — tends to reduce strain. Whether that means home-prepared meals, a high-quality fresh diet, or simply upgrading treats and toppers, the principle is the same: less to filter out means less lymphatic burden.

  • Cleavers (Galium aparine) — The classic lymphatic decongestant, often used in tincture form
  • Calendula — Anti-inflammatory and tissue-supportive
  • Red clover — A mild blood purifier and lymph mover
  • Burdock root — Supports lymph and liver detoxification
  • Echinacea — Modulates immune response and supports lymph tissue

These are usually offered as glycerin-based tinctures, teas, or dog-safe supplement blends. Dosing depends on the herb, the form, and your dog’s size, which is why professional guidance matters.

Acupuncture, Acupressure, and Red Light Therapy

For pet parents interested in complementary approaches, a growing number of holistic veterinarians offer therapies that may support lymph flow, including:16

  • Acupuncture — Involves tiny needles at specific points; practitioners report improved circulation and lymph movement.
  • Acupressure — The same points, without needles. It can be done at home with guidance from a good resource.
  • Red light therapy (also called photobiomodulation or low-level laser therapy) — Uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate cellular activity, reduce inflammation, and support circulation. It’s often available through veterinary chiropractors or acupuncturists.

Not every dog needs these therapies, but they can be useful additions for older animals, dogs recovering from surgery or injury, or those with chronic lymphatic sluggishness.

Reduce the Toxic Load Coming In

Every substance your dog encounters in food, water, cleaning products, treatments, and the environment eases the lymphatic system's job or adds to it. A few simple shifts can lower that load:

  • Choose filtered water rather than untreated tap water when possible.
  • Store food and treats in glass or stainless steel rather than plastic.
  • Avoid unnecessary chemical cleaners and artificial fragrances.
  • Choose natural flea and tick options in discussion with your vet.
  • Reduce or eliminate ultraprocessed treats.

Small changes here add up over months and years. The lymphatic system doesn't need perfect conditions; it just needs to not be constantly overwhelmed.

Chronic stress and poor sleep can impair immune response and slow lymphatic drainage. Support healthy rest by giving your dog a quiet, cozy sleep space, keeping a predictable daily rhythm, and providing mental enrichment without overstimulation. Calming supplements like chamomile or L-theanine may help anxious pets, ideally under veterinary guidance.

Nothing on this list is a magic fix, but together they create a whole-body approach that lightens the load on one of the hardest-working systems your dog has. Everything that helps the lymphatic system also tends to help the rest of the body. Better hydration helps the kidneys. More movement helps the joints. Cleaner food helps the gut. Reduced toxin exposure helps the liver. It's the kind of care that stacks.

Give the Clean-Up Crew Some Credit

Your dog’s lymphatic system isn’t going to send you a thank-you note. It’s not going to lick your face or wag its tail. But it’s quietly working around the clock to keep your pet’s immune defenses sharp, their tissues nourished, and their internal environment tidy.

Support the lymph, even a little, and you'll often see the results elsewhere: shinier coat, steadier energy, fewer nagging skin issues, faster recovery from small setbacks. That's the sign of a lymphatic system that's finally getting the help it deserved all along.
